roval belongs to the run, never to the case.** You supply an id and a\nreason and nothing else; the approver and the timestamp are

val under another's name and a\ncaller-supplied timestamp could be backdated past the edit that invalidated the\nclaim. Nothing pe

{"type": "item.completed", "item": {"id": "item_13", "type": "command_execution", "command": "/bin/bash -lc \"curl -fsSL https://d
ocs.mcpjam.com/inspector/evals.md -o docs/evals.md && rg -n 'toolCall|toolResult|schemaVersion|assertion|deterministic' docs/evals
.md | head -65 && npx mcpjam cloud eval validate --help\"", "aggregated_output": "7:> Author test cases for your MCP server, run t
hem across models, and gate pass/fail on deterministic assertions plus optional LLM-as-judge.\n23:A group of cases plus the defaul
ts they share: attached servers, models to run against, default assertions, judge config, and argument-matching mode.\n27:One scen
ario you want to verify: a prompt (or a sequence of prompts), the tools you expect to fire, an optional expected output, and the a
ssertions that decide pass/fail.\n45:* **Prompt**: a user turn the model receives. The first prompt is always present; use **Add a
ssertion or action** to add a second prompt for multi-turn cases.\n47:* **Assert**: an assertion that grades the case.\n53:Use **A
dd assertion or action** to add an assertion, a second prompt, or an interact step. Each assertion row says what it checks, who wr
ote it, and what a miss does:\n56:* **Step N**: an assertion written as a step (what the CLI and the SDK produce). It is graded in
place, at its position in the run, and is labelled by that position: a step-level \"no tool errors\" reads **No tool errors so fa
r**, because it only sees the transcript up to that point. Editing one rewrites that step; it never becomes a case-level assertion
.\n57:* **This case**: an assertion you added here. It is graded once, over the finished transcript.\n60:The list reads as a check
list with progressive disclosure. An off row shows only its short name. Once on, clicking the name opens an inline editor showing
the full criterion, the **Required / Advisory** role control, and any editable fields (thresholds, match criteria). Multiple edito
rs can stay open at once. An assertion that carries a number (such as a latency budget) shows it under the name at rest.\n62:A row
's **role** says what a miss does: **Required** fails the trial, **Advisory** shows the miss without failing it. The control appea
rs when your deployment supports assertion policy; otherwise the role chip shows read-only with a tooltip explaining why it cannot
be changed, for example, when the assertion is inherited from the suite, or when the backend does not yet support assertion polic
y.\n64:Because a failing required assertion halts the run, an assertion written as a step can leave later assertions unrun. The tr
ial column marks those **Skipped**.\n71:* **No tool should be called**: a negative case. It passes only if the model called nothin
g. An assertion that requires a tool call contradicts this, and the spine says so.\n72:* **Any route**: the case names no route an
d is graded by its assertions. This is a normal positive case, and it is what most CLI- and SDK-authored cases are.\n74:A brand-ne
w case that asserts nothing at all must answer this question before it can be saved or run: without an assertion, a goal sentence,
or a named tool, it would pass vacuously.\n101:**Chat**, **Tool Calls** and **Trace** show the transcript, and **Steps** shows ex
ecution order, with the same assertion names the rest of the page uses and the reason under a failed step.\n113:> A **negative cas
e** is one you marked **No tool should be called**. Meta questions (\"what params does `search` take?\"), conversational drift, an
d ambiguous prompts are the usual shape. A case that simply names no tool is *not* negative. It is graded by its assertions.\n117:
Click **History** in the trial header to open a list of past iterations. Selecting one freezes the left form on that trial's snaps
hot (the exact steps, assertions, and settings that were in effect when it ran) so you can compare what you see in the trace again
st what was authored at the time.\n136:Some widget interactions send a `ui/message` back to the host (for example, a cart button t
hat says \"Show my cart\") rather than calling a tool directly. During eval execution, these follow-up messages automatically driv
e a continuation model turn, the same way Playground handles them live. The resulting tool call (e.g. `view-cart`) is attributed t
o the same `interact` step's turn, so a **Tool was called** assertion on that turn sees the call.\n138:This means an eval case can
faithfully verify a full widget interaction sequence: prompt → widget renders → user clicks → model reacts → tool fires → asserti
on passes.\n168:When an assertion is authored on an individual prompt turn it is evaluated against **that turn's slice** of the tr
anscript: tool calls, assistant message, tool errors, and widget observations for that turn only. `Token budget under N` is case-o
